blocks.content: Instead of laughing at him, she laughed with him. There was a difference. A very dangerous difference.

blocks.speaker: Cassandra
blocks.content: Well, technically Ethan — I think it's good.
He looked back at the canvas, because looking at her directly felt like standing too close to sunlight.
The sentence landed strangely. Simple, casual. But something underneath it stayed.
Ethan looked at her then. For a second, she was not smiling — only a second — then the brightness returned so fast he wondered if he had imagined the absence.
A laugh escaped him before he could stop it. She seemed pleased, like she had won some invisible game.

blocks.speaker: Lena
blocks.content: Cass! We're going to be late.

blocks.speaker: Cassandra
blocks.content: I say a lot of things.

blocks.speaker: Cassandra
blocks.content: I have to go before my friend reports me to myself.
Ethan nodded, unsure what to do with his hands, his face, or the fact that he did not want her to leave.

blocks.speaker: Cassandra
blocks.content: And maybe make the fountain a little less sad.

blocks.speaker: Cassandra
blocks.content: Artists are allowed to be hopeful.
A sentence that sounded playful until it didn't.
Before he could respond, she turned and jogged toward Lena, Winston tucked under her arm. He watched her go. This time, he did not pretend not to.
At the archway she glanced back once. Not long. Just enough. Then she disappeared into the street.
Ethan stood with a brush in his hand and paint on his knuckle, feeling like the whole morning had tilted slightly off center.
He looked back at the canvas. The fountain still looked sad. The bench was empty. But the whole ordinary day no longer felt empty with it.
He dipped the brush and began again. This time, he added warmth to the light.
